title: Test day three
hook: notice what's hard: Guru Nanak's sons refuse a muddy bundle, and Lehna carries it
tomorrow: a host's guests all sent excuses. what did he do with the empty seats?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: easy. Naaman nearly missed a cure for being too simple. Day three of the test asks the other question: what's hard?

Every group has the job nobody volunteers for: the dishes after the party, the phone call nobody wants to make. At Kartarpur, where Guru Nanak lived, the stories tell of a job like that. A bundle of grass for the cattle, cut from a wet field, heavy and dripping mud. The Guru asks his own sons to carry it home. They find reasons not to. And a newer follower, Lehna, in his good clothes, lifts the bundle onto his head and carries it home, mud running down his back.
screen: `THE JOB NOBODY WANTS.` → `A WET BUNDLE AT KARTARPUR.` → `THE SONS SAY NO.` → `LEHNA LIFTS IT.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis, the stories of Nanak's life, say that when someone pointed at the ruined clothes, the Guru said it wasn't mud but saffron, a mark of honor. And when the time came, Guru Nanak passed the Guruship not to his sons but to Lehna, and gave him a new name, Angad. Tradition hears in it ang, a limb: a part of the Guru's own body. The bards in the Guru Granth Sahib sing it plainly: the same light, the same way; only the body changed. That's a Sikh teaching: seva, selfless service, and the hard task done humbly is where the Guru saw who was ready. Here's a neighbor who says something close. In John's Gospel, Jesus takes a towel and washes his students' feet, then says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Shared: the lowly, dirty job is holy work, and whoever does it is honored. And one honest difference. In John, the master stoops to serve the students. In the Sikh story, the student stoops for the master, and becomes the next Guru. So on day three of a test week, notice what's hard. The hard line may be where the rule is actually teaching you.
screen: `NOT MUD, BUT SAFFRON.` · `LEHNA BECOMES GURU ANGAD.` · `JESUS WASHES THEIR FEET.` · `MASTER SERVES, OR STUDENT SERVES.` · then, large: `HARD.`

segments.voice: Name the hardest line of your rule so far. Sit up tall, both feet on the floor, and hold that line in mind the way Lehna held the bundle: steady, not proud, not giving up. Ask what that hard line might be carrying for you. Breathe with it for the rest of the time.
Test day three: notice what's hard, and stay with it a while. Lehna carried the wet bundle the others refused, and the mud was called saffron.
Carry this: hard, the muddy bundle that turned out to be saffron. Day 1693, still carrying.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember that Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to Lehna, renamed Angad, rather than to his sons, and seva, selfless service, is lived out in Sikh life, from the langar kitchen to cleaning the gurdwara. Christians remember Jesus washing his disciples' feet (John 13), and some churches reenact it on Holy Thursday.
